finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id has no authorization enforcement: authorized() returns a boolean that is discarded, so any authenticated user can delete any project they do not own, including by admin-only scope.
finding.source: req.params.id (attacker-controlled path parameter) selects the project at api.js:17; req.user is the requester.

trace.note: Route handler for DELETE /projects/:id; no middleware in this file enforces ownership.
Project fetched by attacker-supplied id with no ownership scoping.
authorized(req.user, project) is called but its boolean return value is ignored, so a non-owner non-admin proceeds.
Project is deleted from the store.
204 returned, confirming success to the attacker.

finding.guards_checked: authorized() (api.js:12-14) returns true/false and never throws, so the check has no effect. authorize() (api.js:4-10) is the throwing variant and is not used on this route. No route-level or router-level middleware is defined in api.js. Upstream auth that populates req.user is not in the repo and could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: api.js:12-14 authorized() exists and returns a boolean, but its result is discarded as a bare statement at api.js:18, so it has no effect. api.js:4-10 authorize() is the throwing variant and is not called on this route. No router or route middleware in api.js enforces ownership.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at api.js:16-20 fetches the project by req.params.id (line 17), calls authorized() at line 18 without testing its return value, and deletes at line 19, so any authenticated user with a valid req.user can delete projects they do not own; the upstream auth that sets req.user is not in the repo, but it is only authentication and does not add an ownership check.

finding.claim: The two admin checks disagree: authorize() uses truthiness of user.isAdmin (line 5) while authorized() requires strict === true (line 13). If isAdmin can be a non-boolean truthy value supplied by the caller or an untrusted token/body, authorize() grants admin rights that authorized() would deny.
finding.source: user.isAdmin, populated by upstream code not in this repo; attacker-controlled only if that population derives from untrusted input such as a JWT claim or request body.
finding.sink: Admin bypass in authorize() at api.js:5, which gates PUT /projects/:id/name at api.js:25.

trace.note: !user.isAdmin is truthy-based; any truthy isAdmin value passes the admin bypass.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() ownerId check (api.js:5) is correct for owners. The inconsistency with authorized() (api.js:13) is the issue. Source of isAdmin is not in the repo, so exploitability depends on that code.

verdict.guard_found: api.js:5 ownerId check (`resource.ownerId !== user.id && !user.isAdmin`) is the only guard on PUT /projects/:id/name (api.js:25). It is a throwing guard, so its result is effective, but the admin branch is the weak point. No other guard exists in api.js. The source of user.isAdmin (api.js:5 and api.js:13) is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: Trace lines 5, 25, and 26 match the claim, and the truthy-vs-`=== true` mismatch between api.js:5 and api.js:13 is real. Whether an attacker can make isAdmin a truthy non-boolean depends on upstream code that populates req.user (not in this repo), so exploitability cannot be decided here. Separately, api.js:18 discards the boolean from authorized(), so DELETE /projects/:id has no effective check at all; that is a different and stronger finding than F2 and is not what the candidate claims.

finding.claim: Existence oracle and error leakage on PUT /projects/:id/name: a nonexistent id makes authorize(user, undefined) throw a TypeError (500) while an existing project owned by someone else returns 403, letting an attacker enumerate valid project ids.
finding.sink: Response status differences from authorize() at api.js:25 and project lookup at api.js:24.

trace.note: Project lookup returns undefined for unknown id.
authorize() reads resource.ownerId on undefined, throwing TypeError (non-403, likely 500).
Existing foreign-owned project yields a deliberate 403 instead.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() ownership check is enforced here. No explicit not-found handling exists. Impact depends on the error handler, which is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. authorize() at api.js:4-10 throws 403 only when resource is non-null and foreign-owned; with resource undefined, api.js:5 throws TypeError before any check. No not-found handling exists at api.js:24-25. The error handler is outside the repo, so the exact status for the TypeError is unverified, but it has no status field and so should default to 500 while the 403 at api.js:7 sets e.status = 403.
verdict.reason: For an authenticated low-privilege user, PUT /projects/:id/name at api.js:24-25 returns 403 for an existing foreign project (api.js:7) but throws a TypeError from api.js:5 for a nonexistent id, so the response status differs and leaks project existence. The attacker only needs a valid session. The impact is low, since the oracle is only useful if project ids are guessable, and it depends on the unseen error handler mapping the two errors to different statuses.

finding.claim: PUT /projects/:id/name returns the entire project object and accepts an unvalidated req.body.name, so any extra fields on the stored project are disclosed to the caller and a non-string or undefined name can be stored.
finding.source: req.body.name (api.js:26) and the stored project record.
finding.sink: Response body at api.js:27 and persisted project.name at api.js:26.

trace.note: req.body.name is assigned without type or presence validation.
res.json(project) serializes the whole record, including any sensitive fields the store holds.

finding.guards_checked: Authorization is enforced by authorize() at api.js:25 before the write. No field allowlist, schema validation, or response projection is applied. The contents of the stored record are not in the repo, so disclosure impact is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:4-10 is called at api.js:25 and throws unless the caller is the project owner or an admin, so the write and response only happen for a caller who already has full access to the project.
verdict.reason: The trace lines are accurate (api.js:26 assigns req.body.name unvalidated, api.js:27 returns the whole project), but the caller must pass authorize() at api.js:25, so they are the owner or an admin who can already read and modify that record, and the repo (only api.js) does not show any stored field the owner is not meant to see, so the disclosure claim has no demonstrated impact; the unvalidated name is at most a data-integrity issue, not a security vulnerability.
